---
name: strix-halo-bench-runs
description: "How the strix-halo-vulkan benchmark suite is run and how long each family takes, plus the run-quality conventions the repo's docs expect."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 6c27486f-644d-4f43-a0b0-6ebe2136679b
  modified: 2026-09-18T12:55:03.680Z
---

`go run ./cmd/bench -blocks 32,64,128,256,512,1024 <family>` — the non-default
block list is what every committed `results/*.csv` was measured with, so keep
it if rows are to stay comparable. `go generate ./...` first if any `.comp`
changed (`*.spv` is gitignored). As of 2026-09-13 the `moe` family is ~9
minutes / 896 rows; it prints its summary tables only at the end, so there is
no progress output to poll — run it in the foreground with a long timeout.
The `bank` family (added 2026-09-15, research/llm-vertical.md L0a) is the odd one out: its 72
timed cells are seconds, but `go run ./cmd/bench -bankgib 64 -bankreadmib 1024
bank` first allocates 64 GiB in 19 buffers and writes one word per 4 KB page,
which is most of its ~3-minute wall clock. Check `free -g` has the headroom
before starting it.

**A whole-model tok/s number is only comparable against a control run the
same hour** (P1c, 2026-09-18): with an identical binary the decode step
measured 30.51 ms one day and 39.20 the next — every *dense-bank* kernel
1.6-1.9x slower (dn.qkv 115→206 us, head 1964→3531) while every MoE
expert-bank rung was unchanged. Suspected GTT page fragmentation of the
float-staged dense banks (32-day uptime, swap 100% full); unprovable without
root. **And a difference below ~0.5 tok/s needs interleaved A/B/A/B pairs, not one
pair** (P3, 2026-09-18): three pairs of the same two banks gave −0.06, +0.14
and +0.05 tok/s, so either single pair would have reported a signed number
where the truth was a within-arm spread of 0.31 against a real difference of
~0.04. Quote the means and the within-arm spread, not one delta.

So when measuring a decode/prefill change, rebuild yesterday's code in
a worktree (`.spv` are gitignored — regenerate or copy them) and run both
binaries back to back; never quote a delta against a prior day's CSV. Also:
run 1 of a freshly staged graph diverges from runs 2+ at ~1.6e-5 in the
logits (research/p1c-prerecorded-decode.md finding 4) — warm the graph once
before any bitwise comparison.

One-token `-ladder` runs of `cmd/llm` (moe/dn/attn/hc) must defeat the 32 MiB
MALL or every rate is an L3 number: stage many layers and use `-iters 1`
(e.g. `-moe -tokens 1 -ladder -layers 16 -iters 1`, P1b 2026-09-18 —
`ProfileSweep` walks a dispatch kind across layers, so each timing reads a
cold bank). The screen: any CSV row whose gbps exceeds 242 was not measuring
DRAM. The default two-layer, 20-iter form re-reads a ~32 MB working set from
the MALL.

**`go generate` after a `.comp` edit is load-bearing, and skipping it fails
*silently and flatteringly*.** `.spv` is gitignored and embedded into the Go
binary, so an edited shader that was not regenerated runs the **previous**
kernel — and a hand-compile to `/tmp` to check syntax is not the same thing.
On 2026-09-19 (P5b) that produced a whole round of measurements that read as a
2x speed-up and a full set of green tests, because the old kernel was doing
half the work on the new grid. Regenerate just the families touched
(`grep "go:generate" shaders/shaders.go | grep <file>.comp | sed 's|^//go:generate ||'`
into a loop) and check the `.spv` mtime before believing any number.

**Why:** the repo's TODO.md handoffs report a reproducibility figure for every
session (two runs of the family, median ratio and p10-p90 over common rows),
so a session that measures anything is expected to run its family twice and
quote the agreement.

**How to apply:** budget ~20 minutes for two `moe` runs, save each log and CSV
to the scratchpad so run N-1 survives for the comparison, and check nothing
else is using the GPU (`/sys/class/drm/card1/device/gpu_busy_percent`) before
starting. **"Nothing else" includes your own `go build` and `go test`** — a
whole-model decode step is ~3 ms of host work in ~28, and compiling beside a
`-gen` run cost one control pass 1.6 tok/s of 35 (P4c, 2026-09-19), which is
four times the difference such a run is usually measuring. Start the
measurement detached (`setsid nohup … &`, or the foreground loop will kill it
when the tool call times out) and edit *text* while it runs, nothing else. Do not poll with `pgrep -f` — see
[[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]].
---
name: llm-resident-run
description: The whole-model runs (`cmd/llm -resident`, `-graph`, `-gen`, `-ppl`, `cmd/serve -llm`, `TestGraphLogits`) stage 82-83 GB of qwen3.8-flash-next; what they cost in time and RAM, and why nothing else can run beside them.
metadata:
  type: project
---

**Since L8a/L8b the dense banks are int8 rather than halves and residency is
81.89 GB with the head** (`-dense` 4.32 GB); `LLM_DENSE_FP16=1` puts every
block back on the old halves and restores the old sizes exactly, which is how
the two are compared. **A decode token is 31.7 ms and residency 79.85 GB as of
L8c-7 (2026-09-17)** with all five 4.5-bit families named in
`LLM_DENSE_BANK` — 40.5 ms at L8e, 33.3 at L8c-6, ~134 before L7d — so `-n 64`
is a ~2.0 s tail on top of staging. Without `LLM_DENSE_BANK` the run is still
L8a's int8 bank at 81.89 GB and 40.5 ms.

**Do not schedule a whole-model run above ~2560 rows**: at 48 layers
`-graph -tokens 3072` (or `-ppl -ctx 4096`) **never returns** — it stalls
inside the driver's submit with one host thread at 100% and the GPU at 2-3%,
and the shim's 20 s fence timeout never fires, so it hangs indefinitely rather
than erroring. 2048 and 2560 are fine; the 4-layer prefix is fine at 4096.
This is a known open question in `research/llm-vertical.md`, not a mistake to re-discover.

`go run ./cmd/llm -resident` (added 2026-09-16, research/llm-vertical.md L6a) stages every layer
of all five blocks: **84.20 GB of device buffers (82.40 since L8a), ~35 s wall
clock**, and it
ends with about 41 GB of MemAvailable left on this 117.7 GiB machine. Peak
host memory is separate — the dense blocks dequantise to f32 before packing,
and the 36 DeltaNet layers are 8.35 GB of transient floats at once — which is
why the tool stages dense first and the 77 GB expert bank last.

**Why:** it is the only thing in the repo that takes most of the machine, so a
second GPU or large-allocation job started beside it will either fail to
allocate or perturb the timing it prints. `-bank N,N,...` restages just the
bank, which is the cheap way to vary residency; `-dense` is the 6.8 GB half
and runs in 8 s.

`go run ./cmd/llm -graph` and `go test ./llm/ -run TestGraphLogits` (added
2026-09-16, research/llm-vertical.md L6b) are the same weight but **85.47 GB**, because they add
the 1.27 GB lm head; `-tokens 2048` adds another ~1.1 GB of arenas. Staging is
~35-40 s, so budget a 1800 s timeout. Both take a `-layers 4` / `GraphOpts{
Layers: 4}` prefix that is 7.4 GB and three seconds — use that while changing
anything about the order, and the full stage only for the gate.

`go run ./cmd/llm -gen` (added 2026-09-16, research/llm-vertical.md L7c) is the same 85.47 GB
plus the KV cache, and it is the slow one: staging is ~35-50 s and generation
is **~40.5 ms a token** (see above), so `-n 64` is a ~2.6 s tail on top.
**Every committed decode CSV is `-prompt 'The capital of France is'`**; the
flag's default is the 81-token `graphDefaultPrompt`, on which the model emits
EOS at the first step and the decode row is meaningless. A 900 s timeout
covers `-n 64`; a two-minute one does not even cover the staging. `-layers 4`
is 7.4 GB, ~2 s to stage and ~18 ms a token, which is the right thing to use
for anything about the loop rather than about the rate.

`go run ./cmd/llm -ppl` (added 2026-09-17, research/llm-vertical.md L8c-0) is the longest of
them: 81.89 GB, ~37 s of staging and then **3.3 s per 2048-token chunk for 145
chunks — 7m58s** over `wiki.test.raw`, so run it in the background and wait on
the log rather than holding a foreground timeout. `-chunks N` cuts it (4
chunks is ~15 s after staging) but **only screens for broken**: four chunks
read +0.32% against llama.cpp where the whole corpus reads −0.13%, sign and
all. `-layers 4` plus `-chunks 2` is the 8 GB plumbing check. The reference
side is `llama-perplexity -c 2048 -b 2048`, ~6.5 s a chunk, and it needs the
machine too — never both at once. **`LLM_DENSE_SIM=<plan>` forces the fp16
arm** (L8c-1), so a simulated run is the old 84 GB residency and ~6 s longer
to stage, and its tok/s means nothing — it grades accuracy only.
`LLM_DENSE_SIM_QUANT=imatrix` needs `models/…/imatrix_unsloth.gguf` (the
fetch script gets it; note the source's `_file` suffix) and adds ~10 s of
staging for the nineteen-rung scale search.

**Since P4b/D20 (2026-09-19) a served-default run also stages the MoE bank
narrower, and it is not free at startup.** `LLM_MOE_BANK` (default off in
`cmd/llm`, set to `llm.ShippedMoEBank` by `cmd/serve -llm`) transcodes four
tensor families out of the checkpoint's bytes — 4.2 B weights of
`ffn_down_exps` plus 236 M of the shared expert — so **the MoE block stages
in ~52 s instead of ~25**, and a whole-model run is ~1m32s to first chunk
rather than ~40 s. Residency drops 77.41 -> 76.00 GB in that block (78.53 GB
whole-model with D19's dense bank). Budget the extra minute in every timeout;
`LLM_MOE_BANK=off` is the control.

`go run ./cmd/serve -llm` (added 2026-09-17, research/llm-vertical.md L9a) is the same residency
held open: **33.5 s to stage at `-llm-ctx 4096`**, ~84 GB, and it then serves
until interrupted. A request is a prefill plus ~44 ms a token (22.7 tok/s
through the server on the L8 banks), so a 48-token answer is under a second.
Start it in the background, poll the log for `listening on`, and **kill it
with `pkill -f '[e]xe/serve'` when finished** — the bracket matters, because
`pkill -f 'exe/serve'` matches the shell running it and kills the session
instead (the same trap as [[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]]). It holds
the machine for as long as it runs. `-llm-layers 4` is the 7 GB, 3.5 s prefix
and is the right thing for anything about HTTP rather than about the text.

**The access log prints no bodies by default** (`-log-bodies` turns them back
on): a chat server's bodies are conversations. The per-request `llm:` line is
separate and always printed — prompt tokens, how many were reused from the
last turn, and the two rates.

**The model path must name a shard, not the directory.**
`models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/` now holds three checkpoints — the model, the
imatrix and the MTP head — so `gguf.OpenSet` refuses it as ambiguous and
`cmd/llm`'s own `-model` default no longer resolves. Pass
`models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00004.gguf`,
which is what `cmd/serve` defaults to.

**`-layers 24` is the end-to-end instrument when 48 will not fit.** With the
`ai` user service resident (~7 GB) this machine has ~80 GB MemAvailable
against a 48-layer `-graph`'s ~80 GB, which is too tight to schedule. A
24-layer `-graph` is **~40 GB, ~2 min to first number**, and it is a *real*
whole-graph measurement — all five blocks, the head, the host loop, the
per-block ms columns in the CSV — not a block bench. Its one distortion is
that the M-independent fixed costs (head 2.4 ms, `ple`, `move`, host) are 24%
of a step there against 13% at 48 layers, so any *ratio* read off it is
optimistic and the 48-layer number is owed (P5, 2026-09-19).

**How to apply:** run them in the foreground with a long timeout and nothing
else on the GPU, the way [[strix-halo-bench-runs]] asks. `-resident`'s closing
measurement (layer 3's MoE block) is comparable to `-moe -tokens 512 -iters 10`
only at the same iteration count.
---
name: llm-bench-needs-bank-cache
description: "Benchmarking cmd/llm on the shipped banks needs LLM_BANK_CACHE set by hand, or every process start re-fits the MoE bank for eight minutes on all 32 cores."
metadata:
  type: project
---

**`cmd/serve` sets `LLM_BANK_CACHE`; `cmd/llm` never does** (the comment at
`cmd/serve/main.go:177` says so outright). So a `cmd/llm` run launched with
`LLM_MOE_BANK` at the shipped plan but no cache path re-fits `ffn_down_exps`
to IQ4_NL from scratch: 40 billion weights through a sixteen-scale search,
`parallelFor` across every core. Measured 2026-09-19: **31 of 32 cores pinned
flat for the whole fit, 5731 CPU-seconds in the first 200 s, sys time 9.3 s**
— all arithmetic, no I/O. research/llm-vertical.md D21 prices the whole fit at ~8 minutes.

Set it and staging is a disk read instead:

    LLM_BANK_CACHE=models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/bank-cache

With it, a 48-layer stage at 131k cells was **58.5 s total, MoE block 19.4 s**,
71.01 GB of weights + 5.09 GB of arenas. The cache directory is 26 GB and was
already complete for the shipped plan (48/48 files per family). It is keyed on
(tensor, shape, source type, target type, arm, version) and lives inside the
checkpoint's directory — it does **not** hash the source bytes.

**The dense bank has no cache at all** (`llm/bank_q4.go`), so it re-fits every
start no matter what. Measured on the same 16 dense layers: banks off **8.6 s
wall / 46.9 CPU-s**, dense bank on **17.4 s / 134.6 CPU-s** — 2.9x the CPU.
That part is unavoidable today.

**Why:** the CPU storm looks alarming and looks like inference gone wrong — it
is neither. It is startup-only weight preparation, which is why the served API
never shows it: the server pays the fit once ever and then holds the model
resident. During real inference the GPU sits at 98-99% and host cost is ~3 ms
of a ~31 ms token.

**How to apply:** set `LLM_BANK_CACHE` in every `cmd/llm` invocation that also
sets `LLM_MOE_BANK`, and budget ~60 s of staging rather than ~8 minutes. See
[[llm-resident-run]] and [[strix-halo-bench-runs]].
---
name: ai-service-user-unit
description: "The ai server runs as a --user systemd unit on :11434; logs are journalctl --user -u ai, deploy.sh installs it, startup takes ~25 s, and it is deliberately served open with -token=."
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
---

The `serve` binary runs as a **user** systemd unit, not a system one, and not
in the foreground:

- **Install/redeploy: `./deploy.sh`.** It builds `./ai` from `./cmd/serve`,
  substitutes the unit's `###` placeholder with `$(pwd)`, writes
  `~/.config/systemd/user/ai.service`, `daemon-reload`s and restarts.
  `./ai.service` in the repo is a *template*, not a script — running it gives
  `Permission denied`, which is the expected outcome, not a bug to fix.
- **`deploy.sh` ends with `journalctl --user -n 100 -f -u ai`,** which never
  returns. In an agent session run its steps by hand and skip the tail.
- **Logs: `journalctl --user -u ai`** (`--user` is required; it is invisible to
  the system journal). The server logs one line per backend at startup and
  `listening on http://0.0.0.0:11434` when all of them are up.
- **Startup is ~25 s** and ~13 GB peak, nearly all of it the Z-Image backend;
  tts/stt/embed land in the first 3 s. Don't conclude anything from the log
  before the image line.
- **State without tailing:**
  `systemctl --user show ai.service -p ActiveState -p SubState -p NRestarts`.
  The unit ships `Restart=always` + `RestartSec=1`, and the server `log.Fatal`s
  on any bad flag or missing checkpoint, so a config mistake becomes a silent
  ~26 s crash loop. A non-zero `NRestarts` (or "restart counter is at N" in the
  journal) is the tell; `systemctl --user reset-failed ai.service` before a
  fixed redeploy so the count reads clean.
- **Auth: omitting `-token` does not disable it.** The flag *defaults* to a
  non-empty token (`defaultToken` in `cmd/serve/main.go`), so a unit that says
  nothing about tokens requires a bearer header on every `/v1` request. Only an
  explicitly empty `-token=` opens the server. This cost an afternoon once.
- **The deployed unit runs `-token=` on purpose**, chosen 2026-09-18: open, no
  bearer header, on `0.0.0.0:11434` so the second machine can reach it. Don't
  "fix" the empty token back to a default — it is the configuration that was
  asked for. See [[deployment-two-machines]].
- The unit is **`disabled`** as of 2026-09-18 — it does not come back on boot
  or login without `systemctl --user enable ai` and `loginctl enable-linger`.

Anchor journal reads to the *current* instance
(`journalctl --user -u ai --since "@$(date -d "$(systemctl --user show
ai.service -p ExecMainStartTimestamp --value)" +%s)"`). A plain `--since -2min`
still contains the previous instance's crash lines and will make an
until-loop fire on a failure that is already fixed — the same self-matching
trap as [[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]]. See
[[deployment-two-machines]] for which box this is meant to run on and
[[gpu-debugging-access]] for when it hangs rather than exits.

**The LLM line (P18, 2026-09-22)** is `-llm -llm-ctx 262144 -llm-batch 8192`: the full trained context, ~66 s and ~83 GB to come up. See [[llm-full-context-262k]].
---
name: llm-full-context-262k
description: "Since P18 (2026-09-22) the LLM holds its full trained 262 144-token context — KV cache is a buffer a plane — and ai.service's LLM line is -llm-ctx 262144 -llm-batch 8192; how it was verified and how to rerun it."
metadata:
  type: project
---

**The server holds 262 144 cells, the model's trained context.** Before P18 the
KV cache shared the attention block's fp16 arena, and `maxStorageBufferRange`
(4 GiB - 4) capped the context at ~148k. Now K, V and the indexer planes are
`kbuf/vbuf/ibuf` at bindings 8-10 (`llm_common.glsl`: `kcache`, `vcache`,
`icache`), and the ceiling is ~349k. `vk/shim.c` `SHIM_MAX_BINDINGS` went from
8 to 16 for it (11 bindings failed as `VkResult(-3)` at `attn.pack`). Write-up:
`research/p18-full-context.md`.

**Verified on the answer, not the rate:**
- `cmd/llm -ppl -ctx 262144 -chunks 1 -ubatch 4096 -head-rows 2048` scores
  positions 131k-262k: **4.0344** (5m27s). `-ubatch` is P18's batched path
  for windows wider than any arena.
- A 237 286-token prompt through HTTP recalls the corpus's first line
  ("Robert Boulter"): prefill 1022 tok/s averaged, decode 29.9 tok/s at 237k.

**Served config (`ai.service`, the commented LLM line):**
`-llm -llm-ctx 262144 -llm-batch 8192`. It stages in ~66 s at ~83 GB, leaving
~33 GB available. It is only the template: this checkout's active line serves the
other four verticals, and the unit is disabled here. See [[ai-service-user-unit]],
[[deployment-two-machines]], [[long-context-prefill-128k]],
[[a-benchmark-that-gets-faster]].

**Depth bench at full length:** `-depth` needs `deepest + len(depths)*(pp+tg)`
cells, so at `-ctx 262144 -pp 4096` use depths `0,248000`.
---
name: deployment-two-machines
description: "Deployment is two Strix Halo machines — LLM on one, the other four verticals on the other — so no cross-vertical footprint work is needed."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: c757bc7f-8b16-44a4-983d-3e1e9e5bd863
  modified: 2026-09-17T23:32:36.559Z
---

Stated by Oliver 2026-09-18: the deployment target is **two** AI MAX+ 395
machines, not one. The qwen3.8-flash-next LLM (~80 GB resident) runs alone on
one; the image/speech/embedding verticals share the other. Consequently:

**Why:** the five-verticals-in-one-process residency problem does not exist,
and quantising z-image (or the other small models) for footprint is not
wanted — the DiT is compute-bound anyway (§3.4), so bits buy no speed.

**How to apply:** don't propose quantisation or memory-coexistence work for
the non-LLM verticals; `research/zimage-vertical.md`'s "What is not planned" section records the
decision. [[phase-2-pivot-to-pipeline]]
---
name: never-edit-source-during-a-sweep
description: "`go run` rebuilds on every invocation, so editing repo source while a multi-arm benchmark script is running kills every arm after the one already in flight."
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

**2026-09-21.** A four-arm 48-layer depth sweep lost three of its four arms.
The script called `go run ./cmd/llm` once per arm; arm 1 had already built and
ran fine; while it ran I edited `shaders/shaders.go` to add a new `//go:embed`
for a `.spv` that did not exist yet, and arms 2-4 each died instantly with

    shaders/shaders.go:2646:12: pattern llm_attn_expand.spv: no matching files found

~25 minutes of measurement, and the failure was silent in the sweep's own log
until the end.

[[strix-halo-bench-runs]] already says "edit *text* while it runs, nothing
else" — that rule is about CPU contention perturbing the numbers. This is a
second, harder reason: **a multi-arm script that invokes `go run` rebuilds the
tree at the start of every arm**, so the source it compiles is whatever the
tree holds *then*, not what it held at launch. Even an edit that compiles
would silently measure a different binary in later arms, which is worse than
a crash.

**How to apply:** make the benchmark script `go build -o <scratchpad>/bench

and +0.05 tok/s, so either single pair would have reported a signed number

~0.04. Quote the means and the within-arm spread, not one delta.

a worktree (`.spv` are gitignored — regenerate or copy them) and run both

name: llm-resident-run
description: The whole-model runs (`cmd/llm -resident`, `-graph`, `-gen`, `-ppl`, `cmd/serve -llm`, `TestGraphLogits`) stage 82-83 GB of qwen3.8-flash-next; what they cost in time and RAM, and why nothing else can run beside them.
metadata:
  type: project
---

**Since L8a/L8b the dense banks are int8 rather than halves and residency is
81.89 GB with the head** (`-dense` 4.32 GB); `LLM_DENSE_FP16=1` puts every
block back on the old halves and restores the old sizes exactly, which is how
the two are compared. **A decode token is 31.7 ms and residency 79.85 GB as of
L8c-7 (2026-09-17)** with all five 4.5-bit families named in
`LLM_DENSE_BANK` — 40.5 ms at L8e, 33.3 at L8c-6, ~134 before L7d — so `-n 64`
is a ~2.0 s tail on top of staging. Without `LLM_DENSE_BANK` the run is still
L8a's int8 bank at 81.89 GB and 40.5 ms.

**Do not schedule a whole-model run above ~2560 rows**: at 48 layers
`-graph -tokens 3072` (or `-ppl -ctx 4096`) **never returns** — it stalls
inside the driver's submit with one host thread at 100% and the GPU at 2-3%,
and the shim's 20 s fence timeout never fires, so it hangs indefinitely rather
than erroring. 2048 and 2560 are fine; the 4-layer prefix is fine at 4096.
This is a known open question in `research/llm-vertical.md`, not a mistake to re-discover.

`go run ./cmd/llm -resident` (added 2026-09-16, research/llm-vertical.md L6a) stages every layer
of all five blocks: **84.20 GB of device buffers (82.40 since L8a), ~35 s wall
clock**, and it
ends with about 41 GB of MemAvailable left on this 117.7 GiB machine. Peak
host memory is separate — the dense blocks dequantise to f32 before packing,
and the 36 DeltaNet layers are 8.35 GB of transient floats at once — which is
why the tool stages dense first and the 77 GB expert bank last.

**Why:** it is the only thing in the repo that takes most of the machine, so a
second GPU or large-allocation job started beside it will either fail to
allocate or perturb the timing it prints. `-bank N,N,...` restages just the
bank, which is the cheap way to vary residency; `-dense` is the 6.8 GB half
and runs in 8 s.

`go run ./cmd/llm -graph` and `go test ./llm/ -run TestGraphLogits` (added
2026-09-16, research/llm-vertical.md L6b) are the same weight but **85.47 GB**, because they add
the 1.27 GB lm head; `-tokens 2048` adds another ~1.1 GB of arenas. Staging is
~35-40 s, so budget a 1800 s timeout. Both take a `-layers 4` / `GraphOpts{
Layers: 4}` prefix that is 7.4 GB and three seconds — use that while changing
anything about the order, and the full stage only for the gate.

`go run ./cmd/llm -gen` (added 2026-09-16, research/llm-vertical.md L7c) is the same 85.47 GB
plus the KV cache, and it is the slow one: staging is ~35-50 s and generation
is **~40.5 ms a token** (see above), so `-n 64` is a ~2.6 s tail on top.
**Every committed decode CSV is `-prompt 'The capital of France is'`**; the
flag's default is the 81-token `graphDefaultPrompt`, on which the model emits
EOS at the first step and the decode row is meaningless. A 900 s timeout
covers `-n 64`; a two-minute one does not even cover the staging. `-layers 4`
is 7.4 GB, ~2 s to stage and ~18 ms a token, which is the right thing to use
for anything about the loop rather than about the rate.

`go run ./cmd/llm -ppl` (added 2026-09-17, research/llm-vertical.md L8c-0) is the longest of
them: 81.89 GB, ~37 s of staging and then **3.3 s per 2048-token chunk for 145
chunks — 7m58s** over `wiki.test.raw`, so run it in the background and wait on
the log rather than holding a foreground timeout. `-chunks N` cuts it (4
chunks is ~15 s after staging) but **only screens for broken**: four chunks
read +0.32% against llama.cpp where the whole corpus reads −0.13%, sign and
all. `-layers 4` plus `-chunks 2` is the 8 GB plumbing check. The reference
side is `llama-perplexity -c 2048 -b 2048`, ~6.5 s a chunk, and it needs the
machine too — never both at once. **`LLM_DENSE_SIM=<plan>` forces the fp16
arm** (L8c-1), so a simulated run is the old 84 GB residency and ~6 s longer
to stage, and its tok/s means nothing — it grades accuracy only.
`LLM_DENSE_SIM_QUANT=imatrix` needs `models/…/imatrix_unsloth.gguf` (the
fetch script gets it; note the source's `_file` suffix) and adds ~10 s of
staging for the nineteen-rung scale search.

**Since P4b/D20 (2026-09-19) a served-default run also stages the MoE bank
narrower, and it is not free at startup.** `LLM_MOE_BANK` (default off in
`cmd/llm`, set to `llm.ShippedMoEBank` by `cmd/serve -llm`) transcodes four
tensor families out of the checkpoint's bytes — 4.2 B weights of
`ffn_down_exps` plus 236 M of the shared expert — so **the MoE block stages
in ~52 s instead of ~25**, and a whole-model run is ~1m32s to first chunk
rather than ~40 s. Residency drops 77.41 -> 76.00 GB in that block (78.53 GB
whole-model with D19's dense bank). Budget the extra minute in every timeout;
`LLM_MOE_BANK=off` is the control.

`go run ./cmd/serve -llm` (added 2026-09-17, research/llm-vertical.md L9a) is the same residency
held open: **33.5 s to stage at `-llm-ctx 4096`**, ~84 GB, and it then serves
until interrupted. A request is a prefill plus ~44 ms a token (22.7 tok/s
through the server on the L8 banks), so a 48-token answer is under a second.
Start it in the background, poll the log for `listening on`, and **kill it
with `pkill -f '[e]xe/serve'` when finished** — the bracket matters, because
`pkill -f 'exe/serve'` matches the shell running it and kills the session
instead (the same trap as [[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]]). It holds
the machine for as long as it runs. `-llm-layers 4` is the 7 GB, 3.5 s prefix
and is the right thing for anything about HTTP rather than about the text.

**The access log prints no bodies by default** (`-log-bodies` turns them back
on): a chat server's bodies are conversations. The per-request `llm:` line is
separate and always printed — prompt tokens, how many were reused from the
last turn, and the two rates.

**The model path must name a shard, not the directory.**
`models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/` now holds three checkpoints — the model, the
imatrix and the MTP head — so `gguf.OpenSet` refuses it as ambiguous and
`cmd/llm`'s own `-model` default no longer resolves. Pass
`models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00004.gguf`,
which is what `cmd/serve` defaults to.

**`-layers 24` is the end-to-end instrument when 48 will not fit.** With the
`ai` user service resident (~7 GB) this machine has ~80 GB MemAvailable
against a 48-layer `-graph`'s ~80 GB, which is too tight to schedule. A
24-layer `-graph` is **~40 GB, ~2 min to first number**, and it is a *real*
whole-graph measurement — all five blocks, the head, the host loop, the
per-block ms columns in the CSV — not a block bench. Its one distortion is
that the M-independent fixed costs (head 2.4 ms, `ple`, `move`, host) are 24%
of a step there against 13% at 48 layers, so any *ratio* read off it is
optimistic and the 48-layer number is owed (P5, 2026-09-19).

**How to apply:** run them in the foreground with a long timeout and nothing
else on the GPU, the way [[strix-halo-bench-runs]] asks. `-resident`'s closing
measurement (layer 3's MoE block) is comparable to `-moe -tokens 512 -iters 10`
only at the same iteration count.

name: llm-bench-needs-bank-cache
description: "Benchmarking cmd/llm on the shipped banks needs LLM_BANK_CACHE set by hand, or every process start re-fits the MoE bank for eight minutes on all 32 cores."
metadata:
  type: project
---

**`cmd/serve` sets `LLM_BANK_CACHE`; `cmd/llm` never does** (the comment at
`cmd/serve/main.go:177` says so outright). So a `cmd/llm` run launched with
`LLM_MOE_BANK` at the shipped plan but no cache path re-fits `ffn_down_exps`
to IQ4_NL from scratch: 40 billion weights through a sixteen-scale search,
`parallelFor` across every core. Measured 2026-09-19: **31 of 32 cores pinned
flat for the whole fit, 5731 CPU-seconds in the first 200 s, sys time 9.3 s**
— all arithmetic, no I/O. research/llm-vertical.md D21 prices the whole fit at ~8 minutes.

Set it and staging is a disk read instead:

    LLM_BANK_CACHE=models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/bank-cache

With it, a 48-layer stage at 131k cells was **58.5 s total, MoE block 19.4 s**,
71.01 GB of weights + 5.09 GB of arenas. The cache directory is 26 GB and was
already complete for the shipped plan (48/48 files per family). It is keyed on
(tensor, shape, source type, target type, arm, version) and lives inside the
checkpoint's directory — it does **not** hash the source bytes.

**The dense bank has no cache at all** (`llm/bank_q4.go`), so it re-fits every
start no matter what. Measured on the same 16 dense layers: banks off **8.6 s
wall / 46.9 CPU-s**, dense bank on **17.4 s / 134.6 CPU-s** — 2.9x the CPU.
That part is unavoidable today.

**Why:** the CPU storm looks alarming and looks like inference gone wrong — it
is neither. It is startup-only weight preparation, which is why the served API
never shows it: the server pays the fit once ever and then holds the model
resident. During real inference the GPU sits at 98-99% and host cost is ~3 ms
of a ~31 ms token.

**How to apply:** set `LLM_BANK_CACHE` in every `cmd/llm` invocation that also
sets `LLM_MOE_BANK`, and budget ~60 s of staging rather than ~8 minutes. See
[[llm-resident-run]] and [[strix-halo-bench-runs]].

name: ai-service-user-unit
description: "The ai server runs as a --user systemd unit on :11434; logs are journalctl --user -u ai, deploy.sh installs it, startup takes ~25 s, and it is deliberately served open with -token=."
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
---

The `serve` binary runs as a **user** systemd unit, not a system one, and not
in the foreground:

- **Install/redeploy: `./deploy.sh`.** It builds `./ai` from `./cmd/serve`,
  substitutes the unit's `###` placeholder with `$(pwd)`, writes
  `~/.config/systemd/user/ai.service`, `daemon-reload`s and restarts.
  `./ai.service` in the repo is a *template*, not a script — running it gives
  `Permission denied`, which is the expected outcome, not a bug to fix.
- **`deploy.sh` ends with `journalctl --user -n 100 -f -u ai`,** which never
  returns. In an agent session run its steps by hand and skip the tail.
- **Logs: `journalctl --user -u ai`** (`--user` is required; it is invisible to
  the system journal). The server logs one line per backend at startup and
  `listening on http://0.0.0.0:11434` when all of them are up.
- **Startup is ~25 s** and ~13 GB peak, nearly all of it the Z-Image backend;
  tts/stt/embed land in the first 3 s. Don't conclude anything from the log
  before the image line.
- **State without tailing:**
  `systemctl --user show ai.service -p ActiveState -p SubState -p NRestarts`.
  The unit ships `Restart=always` + `RestartSec=1`, and the server `log.Fatal`s
  on any bad flag or missing checkpoint, so a config mistake becomes a silent
  ~26 s crash loop. A non-zero `NRestarts` (or "restart counter is at N" in the
  journal) is the tell; `systemctl --user reset-failed ai.service` before a
  fixed redeploy so the count reads clean.
- **Auth: omitting `-token` does not disable it.** The flag *defaults* to a
  non-empty token (`defaultToken` in `cmd/serve/main.go`), so a unit that says
  nothing about tokens requires a bearer header on every `/v1` request. Only an
  explicitly empty `-token=` opens the server. This cost an afternoon once.
- **The deployed unit runs `-token=` on purpose**, chosen 2026-09-18: open, no
  bearer header, on `0.0.0.0:11434` so the second machine can reach it. Don't
  "fix" the empty token back to a default — it is the configuration that was
  asked for. See [[deployment-two-machines]].
- The unit is **`disabled`** as of 2026-09-18 — it does not come back on boot
  or login without `systemctl --user enable ai` and `loginctl enable-linger`.

Anchor journal reads to the *current* instance
(`journalctl --user -u ai --since "@$(date -d "$(systemctl --user show
ai.service -p ExecMainStartTimestamp --value)" +%s)"`). A plain `--since -2min`
still contains the previous instance's crash lines and will make an
until-loop fire on a failure that is already fixed — the same self-matching
trap as [[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]]. See
[[deployment-two-machines]] for which box this is meant to run on and
[[gpu-debugging-access]] for when it hangs rather than exits.

**The LLM line (P18, 2026-09-22)** is `-llm -llm-ctx 262144 -llm-batch 8192`: the full trained context, ~66 s and ~83 GB to come up. See [[llm-full-context-262k]].

name: llm-full-context-262k
description: "Since P18 (2026-09-22) the LLM holds its full trained 262 144-token context — KV cache is a buffer a plane — and ai.service's LLM line is -llm-ctx 262144 -llm-batch 8192; how it was verified and how to rerun it."
metadata:
  type: project
---

**The server holds 262 144 cells, the model's trained context.** Before P18 the
KV cache shared the attention block's fp16 arena, and `maxStorageBufferRange`
(4 GiB - 4) capped the context at ~148k. Now K, V and the indexer planes are
`kbuf/vbuf/ibuf` at bindings 8-10 (`llm_common.glsl`: `kcache`, `vcache`,
`icache`), and the ceiling is ~349k. `vk/shim.c` `SHIM_MAX_BINDINGS` went from
8 to 16 for it (11 bindings failed as `VkResult(-3)` at `attn.pack`). Write-up:
`research/p18-full-context.md`.

**Verified on the answer, not the rate:**
- `cmd/llm -ppl -ctx 262144 -chunks 1 -ubatch 4096 -head-rows 2048` scores
  positions 131k-262k: **4.0344** (5m27s). `-ubatch` is P18's batched path
  for windows wider than any arena.
- A 237 286-token prompt through HTTP recalls the corpus's first line
  ("Robert Boulter"): prefill 1022 tok/s averaged, decode 29.9 tok/s at 237k.

**Served config (`ai.service`, the commented LLM line):**
`-llm -llm-ctx 262144 -llm-batch 8192`. It stages in ~66 s at ~83 GB, leaving
~33 GB available. It is only the template: this checkout's active line serves the
other four verticals, and the unit is disabled here. See [[ai-service-user-unit]],
[[deployment-two-machines]], [[long-context-prefill-128k]],
[[a-benchmark-that-gets-faster]].

**Depth bench at full length:** `-depth` needs `deepest + len(depths)*(pp+tg)`
cells, so at `-ctx 262144 -pp 4096` use depths `0,248000`.

name: never-edit-source-during-a-sweep
description: "`go run` rebuilds on every invocation, so editing repo source while a multi-arm benchmark script is running kills every arm after the one already in flight."
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

**2026-09-21.** A four-arm 48-layer depth sweep lost three of its four arms.
The script called `go run ./cmd/llm` once per arm; arm 1 had already built and
ran fine; while it ran I edited `shaders/shaders.go` to add a new `//go:embed`
for a `.spv` that did not exist yet, and arms 2-4 each died instantly with

    shaders/shaders.go:2646:12: pattern llm_attn_expand.spv: no matching files found

~25 minutes of measurement, and the failure was silent in the sweep's own log
until the end.

[[strix-halo-bench-runs]] already says "edit *text* while it runs, nothing
else" — that rule is about CPU contention perturbing the numbers. This is a
second, harder reason: **a multi-arm script that invokes `go run` rebuilds the
tree at the start of every arm**, so the source it compiles is whatever the
tree holds *then*, not what it held at launch. Even an edit that compiles
would silently measure a different binary in later arms, which is worse than
a crash.

**How to apply:** make the benchmark script `go build -o <scratchpad>/bench
./cmd/llm` **once at the top** and run that binary for every arm. Then the
tree is free to edit while it runs, and every arm is provably the same build.
Select arms with environment variables read at dispatch time (this is what
`LLM_ATTN_SPLITS` and `LLM_ATTN_CELL_SPLITS` are for), never by rebuilding.

lost. There is an `origin` (github.com:theninj4/strix-halo-vulkan) but `main`

session was mid-refactor in `zimage/pipeline` and mid-write in `api/images.go`
while this one built `embed/`: `go build ./...` failed twice on *their*
undefined symbols (`p.latentH`, `formatSize`), minutes apart, and both cleared
on their own. Check `git status --short` and file mtimes before believing a
build break is yours, and build the packages you touched
(`go build ./embed/ ./api/ …`) rather than `./...` while it lasts.

is, and every session appends a handoff to it. That is why the repo's own docs
say to read `TODO.md`/the current vertical file first.

direct-to-main), don't amend the `ai` commits to "improve" them, and put the

targeted replacements rather than whole-file rewrites when another session may

work. See [[strix-halo-bench-runs]] and [[phase-2-pivot-to-pipeline]] for what

1	// Command loadgen is CONCURRENCY.md's C0 harness: it fires voice-shaped and
2	// agent-shaped chat completions at a running server, concurrently, and
3	// reports what each stream saw.
4	//
5	// A **voice** request is a Home-Assistant-shaped system prompt (a fixed list
6	// of rooms and devices, ~2k tokens by default) plus a short utterance, with
7	// thinking off and a short answer. An **agent** request is a long document
8	// from wikitext plus an instruction that produces a long answer. The agents
9	// start at t=0 and the voice requests arrive at -voice-at, so a voice command
10	// lands while the agents are prefilling, decoding, or both.
11	//
12	// Each phase is measured against the same streams run **alone**, the same
13	// hour (-solo, on by default): a concurrent number is only readable next to
14	// its own control.
15	//
16	//	go run ./cmd/serve -llm -llm-ctx 65536 -llm-slots 3 -addr 127.0.0.1:8080 -token= &
17	//	go run ./cmd/loadgen -url http://127.0.0.1:8080
18	//
19	// TTFT is taken at the first delta of any kind (content or reasoning) and the
20	// decode rate is (completion_tokens - 1) over first-to-last delta, with
21	// completion_tokens from the usage frame, so a held-back byte or a hidden
22	// marker moves the edges by a token at most.
23	package main
24	
25	import (
26		"bufio"
27		"bytes"
28		"context"
29		"encoding/json"
30		"flag"
31		"fmt"
32		"io"
33		"log"
34		"net/http"
35		"os"
36		"sort"
37		"strings"
38		"sync"
39		"text/tabwriter"
40		"time"
41	)
42	
43	type stream struct {
44		name   string
45		class  string // "interactive" or "background": sent as X-Priority
46		at     time.Duration
47		system string
48		user   string
49		max    int
50		effort string
51	}
52	
53	type result struct {
54		s             stream
55		start         time.Time
56		first, last   time.Time
57		deltas        int
58		prompt, compl int
59		finish        string
60		err           error
61	}
62	
63	func (r *result) ttft() time.Duration  { return r.first.Sub(r.start) }
64	func (r *result) total() time.Duration { return r.last.Sub(r.start) }
65	
66	// rate is the decode rate the stream saw after its first token.
67	func (r *result) rate() float64 {
68		d := r.last.Sub(r.first).Seconds()
69		if r.compl < 2 || d <= 0 {
70			return 0
71		}
72		return float64(r.compl-1) / d
73	}
74	
75	func main() {
76		url := flag.String("url", "http://127.0.0.1:8080", "server root")
77		token := flag.String("token", "", "bearer token, if the server wants one")
78		corpus := flag.String("corpus", "models/wikitext-2-raw/wiki.test.raw", "text the agent prompts are cut from")
79		agents := flag.Int("agents", 2, "background agent streams, all starting at t=0")
80		agentChars := flag.Int("agent-chars", 32000, "characters of document in each agent prompt (~4 a token)")
81		agentMax := flag.Int("agent-max", 768, "max_tokens of an agent answer")
82		agentClass := flag.String("agent-class", "background", "X-Priority of the agents; empty sends none")
83		voiceAt := flag.String("voice-at", "2s,30s", "comma-separated arrival times of the voice requests, from the agents' start")
84		voiceDevices := flag.Int("voice-devices", 40, "devices in the voice system prompt (~45 tokens each)")
85		voiceMax := flag.Int("voice-max", 32, "max_tokens of a voice answer")
86		voiceClass := flag.String("voice-class", "interactive", "X-Priority of the voice requests; empty sends none")
87		solo := flag.Bool("solo", true, "run each stream alone first, as the control")

input.new_string:
## C0 + C3 — the harness and the chunk curve (measured 2026-09-23)

**The harness is `cmd/loadgen`.** It sends two background agents at t=0
(a 7.3k/7.8k-token wikitext document each, "summarise it at length",
`max_tokens` 768, thinking on) and four interactive voice commands at 2, 9,
25 and 40 s. Each voice command is a Home-Assistant-shaped system prompt of 40
devices (**1.94k tokens**), a short utterance, `reasoning_effort: none` and
`max_tokens` 32. The voice commands at 2 s and 9 s land while the agents are
prefilling, and the ones at 25 s and 40 s land while they are decoding.
Before each concurrent phase it runs every stream alone as the same-hour
control. Every arm below ran the concurrent phase twice, and **the two runs
agree within 0.03 s on every TTFT and 0.3 tok/s on every rate** (the
baseline's within 0.07 s). The server was the 48-layer model at
`-llm-ctx 65536 -llm-batch 8192`, with `ai.service` stopped. The sweep script
restarts the server per arm from one binary.

| arm | voice TTFT at 2 s / 9 s (in prefill) | at 25 s / 40 s (in decode) | agent decode, each | agent prefill alone (7338 tok) | aggregate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| alone (control) | 1.84 / 1.79 | 1.80 / 1.79 | 34.8 | — | — |
| **1 slot (before C2)** | **27.4 / 22.7** | 9.0 / 24.1 | 35.4, but agent1 waits 40.6 s for its first token | 6.32 s (8192 chunk) | 24.8 tok/s |
| 3 slots, chunk 512 | 2.05 / 1.83 | 1.90 / 1.79 | 16.8 | 11.71 s (**+85%**) | 21.3 |
| 3 slots, chunk 1024 | 2.09 / 2.01 | 1.81 / 1.79 | 16.1 | 9.10 s (+44%) | 22.9 |
| **3 slots, chunk 2048** (the default) | 3.41 / 2.44 | 1.81 / 1.79 | 16.2 / 15.7 | 7.29 s (+15%) | 24.2 |
| 3 slots, chunk 4096 | 3.11 / 4.80 | 1.82 / 1.81 | 16.2 / 14.6 | 6.43 s (+2%) | 24.7 |
| 3 slots, chunk 8192 | 5.74 / 7.35 | 1.83 / 1.79 | 13.1 / 15.4 | 6.32 s | 24.8 |

(TTFTs in seconds and rates in tok/s, all as the client sees them.)

What it says:

1. **C2 does what it was for.** A voice command that arrives while the agents
   are decoding gets its solo TTFT and its solo rate (35.4 tok/s against 34.4
   alone) at every chunk size. The agents stall for those ~2 s and nothing
   else happens to them. One that arrives during an agent's prefill waits for
   the chunk on the device and no longer. Before C2 it waited for a whole
   generation, 9-27 s.
2. **Switching slots costs nothing measurable.** The two agents' decode
   windows (~48.8 s for 768 tokens each, minus ~4.4 s of voice turns inside
   them) come to 34.6 tok/s combined, which is the solo rate. Aggregate
   throughput is the same as one slot's to within the prefill-chunk cost, as
   the design said: C2 buys fairness, not tokens. C5 buys tokens.
3. **A prefill chunk has a fixed cost of ~0.39 s**, and it is the MoE bank.
   Fitting chunk time = c0 + n·c1 over the solo prefills gives c0 ≈ 0.39 s
   and c1 ≈ 0.80 ms a token. 0.39 s is one read of the ~76 GB expert bank at
   ~200 GB/s: every chunk of 512 or more rows touches essentially every
   expert. So a chunk under ~2k is mostly bank reading. At 512 the cost is
   +85% on background prefill, and the aggregate falls 14%.
4. **The worst voice wait is one chunk's duration**, not what the two sample
   arrivals happened to hit: ~0.8 s at 512, **~1.3 s at 1024, ~2.0 s at
   2048**, ~3.3 s at 4096 and ~6.3 s at 8192.

**Decision: the default stays 2048.** Going to 1024 saves ~0.7 s of worst-case
voice wait and costs every background prefill 25% (whenever there is more than
one slot, whether or not a voice command ever comes). The larger part of a
voice command's TTFT today is its **own** 1.8 s prefill of a system prompt
that is identical every time, and C4 removes that. Revisit the chunk after C4,
when the chunk wait will be most of what is left. A different lever is the
chunk's fixed cost: if an MoE pass over 1024 rows read less than the whole
bank, small chunks would be cheap, but at 1024 rows × 8 experts of 256 it
does not.

## Next

- **C4 (checkpoints)** is now the biggest lever for voice (1.8 s of a 1.8 s
  TTFT is re-reading the same system prompt). It can be built and gated on
  the 4-layer prefix.

1. **C2 does what it was for.** A voice command that arrives while the agents

   else happens to them. One that arrives during an agent's prefill waits for

content.content:
# P5b — the R-row decode kernels: a two-row pass at 1.17x instead of 3.24x

> **2026-09-19.** P5's design pass found that a verification pass over M rows
> costs **3.24 decode steps at M = 2**, so speculation was a net loss at every
> depth and every acceptance rate, and named the fix: the four decode GEMVs
> with R rows per tile instead of one. P5a then measured the acceptance rate
> at **74.0%** and found the optimum depth to be **1** — a two-row
> verification pass — which scoped this stage from "R general" to **R = 2**.
>
> **Built and measured. A two-row pass is 19.5 ms against 16.6 at one row —
> 1.17x, against the 1.16x the design pass projected — where it was 54.1.**
> One row is unregressed at 16.6 against 16.7, which matters more than the
> headline: that is the product decode path.

Data: `results/p5b_graph_m.csv` against `results/p5_graph_m_r1.csv`.
Code: `shaders/llm_gemv.comp`, `llm_hc_gemv.comp`, `llm_moe_gemv.comp`,
`llm_moe_router.comp`, and `GEMVMaxRows` in `llm/bank.go`.

---

## 1. The measurement

`-graph -tokens 1,2,3,4,6,8 -layers 24 -ctx 2048`, D19 dense bank + D20/D21
MoE bank, the same configuration P5's baseline was taken on:

| M rows | before | after | | hc | ple | dn | attn | **moe** | head |
|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 16.7 | **16.6** | 1.00x | 2.1 | 0.3 | 4.0 | 1.3 | 5.3 | 2.4 |
| **2** | **54.1** | **19.5** | **1.17x** | **2.0** | 0.3 | **4.1** | **1.2** | **8.2** | 2.4 |
| 3 | 58.3 | 57.6 | 3.47x | 14.0 | 0.3 | 8.7 | 2.7 | 28.5 | 2.4 |
| 4 | 59.6 | 60.1 | 3.62x | 14.1 | 0.3 | 9.0 | 2.7 | 30.7 | 2.4 |
| 6 | 65.4 | 65.2 | 3.93x | 13.9 | 0.3 | 8.5 | 2.7 | 36.4 | 2.4 |
| 8 | 72.1 | 72.7 | 4.38x | 14.0 | 0.3 | 8.7 | 2.7 | 43.5 | 2.4 |

Rows 3 and up are **unchanged by construction**: `GEMVMaxRows` is 2, so the
host still falls back to the GEMM there, and the fact that those rows land
within 1% of the baseline is the cheapest available check that nothing else
moved.

Per block, cold-bank ladders at the rung the model runs:

| block | ×N | M=1 before → after | M=2 before → after | M=2/M=1 now |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|
| hyper_conn | 97 | 55.6 → 78.9 us | 273.1 → **40.3** | 0.51x |
| deltanet | 36 | 201.1 → 197.8 | 428.5 → **191.8** | 0.97x |
| full_attn | 12 | 230.4 → 239.4 | 420.9 → **197.3** | 0.82x |
| moe | 48 | 196.2 → 204.7 | 1149.3 → **329.2** | 1.61x |

(the M = 1 column moves by up to 1.4x between runs on `hc` and `dn` — these
are the smallest dispatches in the model and P1b's environment gap is at its
widest here. The M = 2 column and the whole-graph table are what the argument
rests on. Only one whole-graph run was taken rather than the usual two: the
effect is 2.8x and run-to-run spread on this instrument is a few per cent.)

### Finding 1 — three of the four blocks are *faster* at two rows than at one

`hc` 0.51x, `dn` 0.97x, `attn` 0.82x. Not "flat" — **faster**. The weight
traffic is identical, and the second row gives the memory system a second
independent stream of A loads to overlap against the same bank read, on
dispatches that were latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound at one row.

content.content:
type: feedback
---

When a change makes the model run at a **new row count** — P5b's R-row decode
GEMVs, P6 raising `GEMVMaxRows`, anything touching `MAXROWS` — add that count
as a rung to `TestGraphIsAChunkSplit` **in the same commit**. A prompt run in
chunks of R has to be the prompt run whole, and that is the only gate in the
suite that sees the whole graph at R rows.

P5b shipped R = 2 with four new block tests, all green. P5c then ran the graph
two tokens at a time and it did not reproduce the prompt, three separate ways:
the schedule pin silently stopped pinning at two rows, the four MoE expert
dispatches never named their row-specialized pipeline (so every two-row batch
ran the one-row kernel — 45x on the residual), and the R-row GEMV re-read the
bank per row. The chunk-split test ran 128, 9 and 1 and skipped straight over 2.

**Why:** a block test compares a new path against an old one over an arena the
old one just wrote, so a kernel that leaves a row unwritten passes; and a
"changing the input moves the output" control can be satisfied by a *later*
stage of the block (the MoE's combine re-reads a different expert set) while
the stage under test does nothing. Only the whole graph, continued, has no
such alibi.

**How to apply:** add the rung, and when a block test is the thing being
relied on, make the reference pass not be the last thing that wrote the buffer
— dirty it with different input in between. See
[[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]] for the other shape of this: a check
that cannot fail is not a check.

input.old_string:
## Next

- **C4 (checkpoints)** is now the biggest lever for voice (1.8 s of a 1.8 s
  TTFT is re-reading the same system prompt). It can be built and gated on
  the 4-layer prefix.
- **C5a** (price a 3-row pass at 48 layers) needs the machine. C5 itself is

input.new_string:
## C5a — what a three-row pass costs (measured 2026-09-23)

`cmd/llm -graph -tokens 1,2,3 -layers 48 -ctx 2048` on the shipped banks
(`LLM_DENSE_BANK`/`LLM_MOE_BANK` as `cmd/serve` sets them, plus
`LLM_BANK_CACHE`). Two builds, interleaved A/B/A/B: HEAD, where
`GEMVMaxRows` is 2 and a three-row pass falls back to the GEMM, and a scratch
worktree with `MAXROWS 3` in the four GEMV shaders and `GEMVMaxRows = 3`.
The two pairs agree within 1 ms.

  three streams would get **~19 tok/s each (57 aggregate)** against ~11.5

  ~26 tok/s each and 51 aggregate.

  attn, ple and head are all within 0.4 ms from one row to three. **The MoE
  is the whole cost**, and `moe.up` alone goes 6.0 → 14.8 → 24.0 ms. More
  rows touch more distinct experts, so some of that growth is bytes that must
  be read. But `moe.up` grows 4.0x over three rows, while `moe.down` over the
  same expert set grows 2.3x (2.6 → 6.0 ms). `moe.up` at R rows is the kernel

  loop is parked), and one row is unchanged, so C5 can raise it. It has to

  1e-3). The existing "3 at a time" rung runs on the pinned schedule, so it
  would not see a broken three-row GEMV. **C5's commit should carry these two
  subtests.**

  voice stream 1.33x (35 → ~26 tok/s) and two cost it 1.78x (→ ~20 tok/s). A
  spoken reply is consumed at speech rate, which is well under either, so
  riding is plausible for TTS-bound replies. It stays a knob, and it defaults
  to off, until C5 exists.

  the 4-layer prefix.

2	
3	> **Opened 2026-09-23.** This is the live file for P6 ("batching"), which
4	> `TODO.md` and `research/llm-vertical.md` carried as *blocked on the product
5	> question: will the API serve more than one stream?* **The answer is yes**:
6	> **three concurrent completions**, as fair as the hardware allows, with a
7	> **priority lane** for a latency-bound caller (a voice command) over
8	> callers that can wait a few seconds (background agents). Like `TODO.md`,
9	> this file is rewritten rather than appended to; a closed stage's write-up
10	> goes to `research/` when it is long.
11	
12	## Where it started (before C2)
13	
14	`backend.LLM` held **one `llm.Graph`, one sequence and one mutex for the
15	whole request** (`backend/llm.go`, `Complete`). A second request waits for
16	the first to finish generating, and the log line says so (`(Ns queued)`). The
17	device lock is taken per forward pass, but the graph lock is held per request,
18	because the graph's carried state *is* the conversation:
19	
20	| per-sequence state | where | size |
21	|---|---|---|
22	| KV cache: K, V, indexer raw + pooled keys | `AttnGPU.kbuf/vbuf/ibuf`, 12 layers | **27.8 KB a cell**: 7.25 GB at 262 144 cells |
23	| DeltaNet recurrent state | `DeltaNetGPU.aState`, 36 layers | 113.25 MB |
24	| DeltaNet convolution rings | `DeltaNetGPU.aWin` | 7.13 MB |
25	| PLE convolution ring | `PLEGPU.aHist` | small |
26	| position | `SEQ_PAST`, dword 0 of three blocks' arenas | 4 bytes |
27	| token ids (n-gram gather) | `Graph.ids` | host |
28	| the recorded decode step (P1c) | `Graph.pre` | its push constants hold the offsets above |
29	
30	Everything else in the graph is **per pass**, not per sequence: the hyper-connection
31	residual, the MoE, the head and every activation arena are rewritten from
32	scratch by each pass. So a second sequence needs a second copy of the table
33	above and nothing else.
34	
35	Prefix reuse was **one sequence deep and all-or-nothing** (and within a slot it still is). A
36	DeltaNet state has no inverse, so a conversation that diverges from the held
37	one anywhere before its end is prefilled from token zero. That already costs
38	the voice case today: a Home Assistant command is the same long system prompt
39	plus a new utterance. The held sequence is the *previous* utterance and its
40	answer, so every command re-reads the system prompt.
41	
42	### The numbers this plan is priced against
43	
44	- **Decode: 34.2 tok/s through the server** (~29 ms a step), and the step is
45	  *latency, not bandwidth*: single-wave workgroups that all fit at once (P8).
46	  That is why rows are cheap. **A two-row pass costs 1.32 steps at 48 layers**
47	  (P5c), and the MoE is the part that keeps growing (10 experts touched at
48	  M = 1, 17 at 2, 36 at 4).
49	- **Prefill: ~1200 tok/s**, and a unit of work is a whole `-llm-batch` chunk.
50	  At the served 8192 that is **~6-7 s that nothing else can interrupt**.
51	- **Memory:** the served 262k configuration stages at ~83 GB and leaves ~33 GB.
52	  Two more full-context sequences would need 14.5 GB of KV plus 0.24 GB of
53	  DeltaNet state. That fits, with ~18 GB to spare.
54	- **`maxStorageBufferRange` is 4 GiB - 4**, and a K or V plane is 12 KB a cell,
55	  so **one plane buffer holds ~349k cells in total**. If slots share a buffer
56	  by offset, `slots × ctx ≤ ~349k` (for example 3 × 112k). Three full 262k
57	  contexts need a buffer per slot, bound as a descriptor array (C6), like the
58	  MoE bank's.
59	
60	## The design, in one paragraph
61	
62	**Slots, then a scheduler, then batching.** The graph gets `S` *sequence
63	slots*: `S` copies of the per-sequence state above, one live at a time,
64	switched by `Graph.UseSlot` (C1). The backend replaces its mutex with a
65	**scheduler that owns the graph** and interleaves *work units*: a decode step
66	or a prefill chunk, each on some slot. It picks the next unit by priority
67	class and then round-robin (C2). This is concurrency without extra
68	throughput: three streams share ~34 tok/s. What it buys is that nobody waits
69	for someone else's whole generation, and a voice command waits at most one
70	work unit. Making that unit short is C3. **Batching (C5)** then runs the
71	decoding slots' next tokens as **R rows of one pass**. Every block but
72	attention, DeltaNet and PLE is already row-independent, and P5b built the
73	R-row decode GEMVs. It is the step that adds throughput: if three rows cost
74	~1.5 steps, three streams get ~23 tok/s each instead of ~11.
75	**Checkpoints (C4)** make prefix caching work across more than one live
76	conversation, and between the turns of a voice session.
77	
78	## Priority
79	
80	Two classes, **interactive** and **background**. The API names the class:
81	
82	- `service_tier` on the request body (OpenAI's field on chat completions and
83	  responses): `"priority"` is interactive; `"flex"`, `"default"` or absent
84	  are background, unless the server's default says otherwise.
85	- An `X-Priority: interactive|background` header, for a client that cannot
86	  add a body field (Home Assistant's OpenAI integration is the likely one).
87	- A server flag for the default class.
88	
89	Scheduling rules (C2, tuned in C3):
90	
91	1. An interactive unit always runs before a background one. Preemption
92	   happens at a **unit boundary**, never mid-pass. The activation arenas are
93	   shared, so a pass cannot be paused.
94	2. Within a class, round-robin **by GPU time**, not by unit count (deficit
95	   round-robin). A prefill chunk is worth ~200 decode steps.

97	   is more than one slot. It cannot wait until an interactive request is live,
98	   because by then the chunk it waits behind has already started. So the worst
99	   wait an interactive request sees is one short chunk rather than 6-7 s, and
100	   what that costs background prefill is C3's measurement.

3	// The language model's scheduler (CONCURRENCY.md C2).
4	//
5	// One graph, several conversations. The graph holds `Slots` sequences
6	// (llm.GraphOpts.Slots, C1) and runs one pass at a time, so concurrency here
7	// is interleaving: a request holds a slot for its whole life, and its work
8	// reaches the device as **units** — one prefill chunk or one decode step —
9	// that a single goroutine picks from every live request's queue in turn.
10	// Nobody waits for another conversation's whole generation any more; they
11	// wait for one unit of it.
12	//
13	// Which unit runs next is the whole policy:
14	//
15	//  1. **Interactive before background, strictly.** While an interactive
16	//     request holds a slot, no background unit starts — including in the
17	//     millisecond between two of its decode steps, when it is sampling and
18	//     has nothing queued. Without that rule a background chunk slips into
19	//     every gap and the voice reply runs at half rate or worse.
20	//  2. **Within a class, whoever has had the least device time.** A prefill
21	//     chunk is worth hundreds of decode steps, so counting units would hand
22	//     a long prompt the device; counting time shares it.
23	//  3. **A background prefill runs in chunks of PreemptChunk**, because a
24	//     unit cannot be interrupted once it is on the device (the activation
25	//     arenas are shared), and an interactive request can arrive at any
26	//     moment. The served -llm-batch 8192 is ~7 s a chunk; the quantum is
27	//     what bounds a voice command's wait.
28	//
29	// Slots are handed out on the same order, and a slot is reserved for the
30	// interactive class when there is more than one, so that background agents
31	// can never occupy every slot and lock a voice command out.
32	//
33	// **Each slot also keeps a checkpoint** (C4): its carried state at the end of
34	// everything before the last user turn of the last request it ran. The next
35	// voice command on the same system prompt, or the next turn of a
36	// conversation whose re-rendered history no longer matches what was
37	// generated, restores it and prefills only what follows. The prefill chunk
38	// is cut at that boundary so the checkpoint can be taken there.

162		running *llmUnit
163		arrival uint64
164		closed  bool
165		stopped chan struct{}
166	}

168	func newLLMSched(g *llm.Graph, dev *Device, batch, preempt, reserve int) *llmSched {
169		s := &llmSched{
170			g: g, dev: dev, batch: batch, preempt: preempt, reserve: reserve,
171			slots: make([]llmSlot, g.Slots()), stopped: make(chan struct{}),
172		}
173		s.wake = sync.NewCond(&s.mu)
174		go s.loop()
175		return s
176	}
177	
178	// acquire waits for a slot and claims it. The job it returns must be
179	// released, whatever happens after.
180	func (s *llmSched) acquire(ctx context.Context, class llmClass, ids []int32, mark int) (*llmJob, error) {
181		s.mu.Lock()
182		if s.closed {
183			s.mu.Unlock()
184			return nil, fmt.Errorf("the language model is closed")
185		}
186		s.arrival++
187		j := &llmJob{ctx: ctx, class: class, slot: -1, arrival: s.arrival, prompt: ids, mark: mark,
188			granted: make(chan struct{})}
189		s.waiting = append(s.waiting, j)
190		s.grant()
191		s.mu.Unlock()
192	
193		select {
194		case <-j.granted:
195			return j, nil
196		case <-ctx.Done():
197			s.mu.Lock()
198			defer s.mu.Unlock()
199			if j.slot >= 0 {
200				// Granted in the meantime; give it straight back.
201				s.releaseLocked(j)
202				return nil, ctx.Err()
203			}
204			s.dropWaiter(j)
205			return nil, ctx.Err()
206		}
207	}
208	
209	// grant hands free slots to waiting jobs, best first.
210	func (s *llmSched) grant() {
211		for {
212			w := s.bestWaiter()
213			if w == nil {
214				return
215			}
216			slot := s.freeSlot(w.class, w.prompt)
217			if slot < 0 {
218				return
219			}
220			s.claim(w, slot)
221		}
222	}
223	
224	// bestWaiter is the waiting job a free slot goes to: interactive first, then
225	// the oldest.
226	func (s *llmSched) bestWaiter() *llmJob {
227		var best *llmJob
228		for _, w := range s.waiting {
229			if best == nil || w.class < best.class || (w.class == best.class && w.arrival < best.arrival) {
230				best = w
231			}
232		}
233		return best
234	}

p="CONCURRENCY.md"; s=open(p).read()
def rep(a,b):
    global s
    assert s.count(a)==1, a
    s=s.replace(a,b)
rep('| **C4** | **Checkpoints: prefix caching across threads** |',
    '| ~~**C4**~~ | ~~**Checkpoints: prefix caching across threads**~~ **done 2026-09-23** within a slot (below); cross-slot restore not built |')
rep('''## Next

- **C4 (checkpoints)** is now the biggest lever for voice: 1.8 s of a 1.8 s
  TTFT is re-reading the same system prompt. It can be built and gated on
  the 4-layer prefix.
- **C5 (batched decode)**''','''## C4 — checkpoints (done 2026-09-23)

`llm.Graph.Checkpoint` / `Restore`, and a checkpoint per slot in the
scheduler.

- **What a checkpoint is.** It holds the live slot's DeltaNet state and rings
  for every layer (~120 MB at 36 layers), the PLE ring, the position and the
  ids, copied on the host. The arenas are host-cached and mapped, so this is
  a memcpy, not a readback. The KV cells and raw indexer keys below the
  position stay on the device, because a continuation from there never
  rewrites them. So a checkpoint restores only into its own slot, and only
  while that slot's ids still start with the checkpoint's. `Restore` checks
  both and refuses otherwise.
- **The pooled indexer table needs no restore**, although P5c's rollback
  snapshots it. The first version restored it, and its control did not
  move. The reason is in `llm_attn_score.comp`: a pass rebuilds the blocks it
  completes before it scores any. Every block at or past the last whole one
  is scored as one broadcast value under a −inf or 1e9 bias (P7), and no
  stored row can change that selection. So the restore was dropped, and the
  gate keeps the case that could have disproved this (below).
- **Where the checkpoint goes.** It sits at the end of everything before the
  last `<|im_start|>user` (`backend.checkpointAt`). That point is found on
  the rendered text and re-encoded, and refused if the result is not a token
  prefix of the prompt. A prefix under 256 tokens is not checkpointed. The
  scheduler cuts the prefill chunk at the boundary and checkpoints after it,
  reusing the slot's host buffers. Slot choice counts a restorable checkpoint
  as reuse, and among slots that save a job nothing it overwrites the one
  with the least checkpointed first. Without that, agents arriving after a
  voice command take its slot by LRU. `-llm-checkpoints=false` is the
  control. The log says `(N from a checkpoint)` where it said `(N cached)`.

**Gates:**
- `TestGraphCheckpointIsThePrefill` (4 layers, 7 s): a 2600-token prefix in
  a 4096-cell cache (sparse: the selection is past its width), checkpointed
  in slot 1. The slot then runs a 600-token detour and 12 steps, slot 0 runs
  another conversation, and slot 1 restores and runs a 300-token tail and 12
  steps. **All 13 logit rows are bit-identical** to prefix + tail run
  directly. The detour runs further than the real continuation, so stale
  pooled blocks are present at the decode frontier, and they still change
  nothing. Controls: a restore without the DeltaNet state moves row 0 (logit
  0 −0.8748 against −0.8638), and one without the PLE ring moves row 0 too
  (−0.8640). `Restore` refuses a slot that has since been re-run from token
  zero.
- `TestLLMCheckpointIsTheSystemPrompt` (backend, 4 layers): a voice-shaped
  request restores the system prompt's checkpoint (566 of 585 tokens,
  prefill 148 → 24 ms) and streams exactly the text of a fresh prefill. The
  scheduler's restore counter is asserted, so a run that never restored
  cannot pass.

**At 48 layers** (C0's harness, 3 slots, same hour, two runs agreeing within
0.02 s):

| | voice alone | voice during agent prefill (2 s / 9 s) | during agent decode (25 s / 40 s) | agents done | aggregate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| chunk 2048, checkpoints off | 1.83 s | 3.41 / 2.44 | 1.80 / 1.79 | 66.3 s | 24.1 tok/s |
| **chunk 2048, checkpoints on** | **0.19 s** | 1.82 / 1.11 | **0.22 / 0.20** | 59.9 s | 26.7 |
| chunk 1024, checkpoints on | 0.19 s | **0.50 / 1.14** | 0.22 / 0.21 | 63.5 s | 25.2 |

- **A voice command's TTFT goes from 1.83 s to 0.19 s**: 1917 of its ~1940
  tokens come from the checkpoint, and what is left is a ~22-token pass plus
  the restore. The first command after a start pays **+0.2 s once** (2.03 s):
  the checkpoint copy and the extra chunk the cut makes.
- Voice turns are cheaper, so the agents finish 6.4 s sooner and the aggregate
  rises 11%.
- **The chunk wait is now nearly all of a voice command's latency while an
  agent prefills.** At 2048 the wait is up to ~2.0 s, plus ~0.2 s. At 1024
  it is up to ~1.3 s, and the price is the +25% background prefill C3
  measured (agents 3.6 s later here, aggregate −6%). That is the decision
  C3 deferred, and it is now a product call (open question below).

**Not built: cross-slot restore.** A checkpoint restores only into its own
slot. Copying the KV cells too (27.8 KB a cell, ~53 MB for a 1.9k system
prompt) would let a voice command use a checkpoint while another voice
command holds its slot. It is not needed while one slot is reserved for the
interactive class and commands arrive one at a time.

## Next

- **C5 (batched decode)**''')
rep('''- **How long is Home Assistant's system prompt?** C4's value and C3's chunk
  cap both depend on it. One real request in the journal answers it.''','''- **How long is Home Assistant's system prompt?** C4's value and C3's chunk
  cap both depend on it. One real request in the journal answers it. The
  harness assumes 1.94k tokens (40 devices).
- **The preempt chunk, 2048 or 1024?** With C4 in, it decides a voice
  command's worst wait while an agent prefills (~2.2 s against ~1.5 s), and
  1024 costs every background prefill 25%. The default is still 2048.''')
rep('''- **2026-09-23**: C0 (`cmd/loadgen`), C3's chunk curve, C1's depth check at
  99k in slot 1, and C5a, all on the 48-layer model with `ai.service`
  stopped. The chunk stays at 2048, and C4 is next.''','''- **2026-09-23**: C0 (`cmd/loadgen`), C3's chunk curve, C1's depth check at
  99k in slot 1, and C5a, all on the 48-layer model with `ai.service`
  stopped. The chunk stays at 2048.
- **2026-09-23**: **C4 done** (within a slot). The voice TTFT goes from 1.83
  to 0.19 s at 48 layers.''')
open(p,"w").write(s)
EOF

content.content:
nothing: between two decode steps there is no work in flight. What is held for
the length of a request is a *slot* of the graph, whose cache, PLE ring and
DeltaNet state are one sequence's.

**`-llm-slots N` holds N conversations at once** (CONCURRENCY.md, C1/C2). Each
slot is its own KV cache (27.8 KB a cell), DeltaNet state and rings (120 MB);
the cache planes' 4 GiB range caps `slots x -llm-ctx` at ~349k cells. A
request holds one slot for its life, and a scheduler interleaves every live
request's work a **unit** at a time — one prefill chunk or one decode step.
This is concurrency and not throughput: three streams share one stream's
~34 tok/s until batched decode (C5) lands. The order is:

1. **Interactive before background, strictly.** A request is interactive if
   it sends `X-Priority: interactive` or `service_tier: "priority"`, and
   background with `X-Priority: background` or `service_tier: "flex"`;
   otherwise `-llm-class` decides (background by default). While an
   interactive request holds a slot no background unit starts, so a voice
   command decodes at the full single-stream rate. Measured on the 4-layer
   prefix: a 16-token interactive request beside two decoding background ones
   finished in 166 ms, against 419 ms sharing with them as an equal.
2. **Within a class, the least device time served goes first**, so a long
   prompt cannot take the device from a conversation that is decoding.
3. **A background prefill runs in `-llm-preempt-chunk` pieces** (2048), because
   a unit cannot be interrupted once it is on the device and an interactive
   request can arrive at any moment.

`-llm-reserve` (1) slots are only for interactive requests, so background
agents can never occupy every slot. A request that finds no slot it may take
waits for one, and the log line says `(Ns queued)`. With more than one slot the
line also names the slot, the class and how long the request's units
`stalled` behind other conversations'.

**Parakeet is resident.** `-stt` stages the encoder and the transducer tail
once, sized for `-max-audio` seconds (60 by default), and every shorter clip
runs in the same arenas — `UploadMel` settles the geometry per run. A request
costs a front end on the host and two submits. A longer clip is refused with a
    -llm-model       models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/…-00001-of-00004.gguf
    -llm-ctx         4096         cache cells: the longest conversation, prompt plus completion
    -llm-batch       4096         tokens the prefill arenas hold (P16: wider costs memory only)
    -llm-max-tokens  1024         what a request that names no max_tokens gets
    -llm-layers      0            stage the first N layers only; a fast start, not an answer
    -llm-slots       1            conversations held at once; slots x ctx <= ~349k cells
    -llm-preempt-chunk 2048       longest background prefill chunk, with more than one slot
    -llm-reserve     1            slots only interactive requests may take, with more than one
    -llm-class       background   priority of a request that names none

    -tts         false            load Kokoro-82M
    -tts-model   models/Kokoro-82M
    -tts-gpu     false            stage per utterance; see above
attention cache is masked by position and both convolution rings are addressed
by it, so those would survive, but a DeltaNet layer's recurrent state is a
running product with no inverse. So the prefix has to be the whole of what is
held, or the sequence starts again. A miss costs one comparison; a hit costs
nothing and saves the history.

With `-llm-slots 1` **the graph is one conversation's**: two clients are
served correctly — the second waits, and re-prefills — but they take turns
evicting each other's prefix. With more slots each holds its own, and a
request is given the free slot already holding the longest prefix of its
prompt, else the least recently used one. The reuse is still all-or-nothing
within a slot; checkpoints that survive a divergence are CONCURRENCY.md's C4.

## One prompt, three envelopes, and a template that is not ours

The three chat endpoints are one generation. `/v1/chat/completions` is
OpenAI's, `/v1/responses` is OpenAI's newer one, `/v1/messages` is
Anthropic's, and each is a translation into the same `api.CompletionRequest`
and back out of the same token stream. Nothing but the envelope differs, which
is why the tests for two of them are about the translation and not about the
model.

They do disagree about **reasoning**, and usefully. A chat completion carries
it in a `reasoning_content` field beside the content — not OpenAI's field, but

---
name: concurrency-loadgen-run
description: "How CONCURRENCY.md's C0 harness (cmd/loadgen) is run against a 48-layer server: a sweep script restarting cmd/serve per arm, ~4.5 min an arm, and what its numbers are sensitive to."
metadata:
  type: project
---

`cmd/loadgen` (added 2026-09-23, CONCURRENCY.md C0) is an HTTP client: two
background agents (7.3k/7.8k-token wikitext prompts, 768 tokens out) at t=0,
and voice commands (a 1.94k-token Home-Assistant-shaped system prompt, 40
devices, `reasoning_effort: none`) at `-voice-at 2s,9s,25s,40s`. It runs every
stream alone first as the same-hour control, then `-runs 2` concurrent phases.

**An arm is a server configuration, so the sweep restarts `cmd/serve` per
arm:** build `serve` and `loadgen` once into the scratchpad (see
[[never-edit-source-during-a-sweep]]), start the server at
`-llm -llm-ctx 65536 -llm-batch 8192 -addr 127.0.0.1:8080 -token=` plus the
arm's flags, wait for `listening on` while checking the PID, run loadgen, and
kill the PID. **~65 s to stage plus ~3.5 min of load is ~4.5 min an arm.**
The two concurrent runs agree within ~0.03 s, so one pair per arm is enough.
It needs `ai.service` stopped (the server is ~83 GB), per [[llm-resident-run]].

**Why:** the voice TTFT during an agent's prefill is set by *where the arrival
lands inside a prefill chunk*. The two sampled arrivals are not the worst
case, which is one whole chunk (~2.0 s at 2048, ~1.3 s at 1024). A prefill
chunk has a fixed ~0.39 s cost (one read of the MoE bank), which is why small
chunks are expensive.

**How to apply:** quote the worst-case wait from the chunk duration, not from
the two samples. Remember that the first voice command after a start pays for
the checkpoint (+0.2 s once), and later ones restore it (0.19 s TTFT since C4).

content.text:
C0, C3, C4 and C5a are done, and C1's item that was owed a depth check now has one. All numbers are 48-layer, and both runs of every arm agree within ~0.03 s.

**C0: the load generator (`cmd/loadgen`).** It sends two long-prompt agents plus four voice commands (a ~1.9k-token Home-Assistant-style system prompt).
- With today's single slot, a voice command waited **9-27 s** for a first token, against 1.8 s alone.
- With 3 slots and C2's scheduler, it waits one prefill chunk if an agent is prefilling, and nothing at all if the agents are decoding.
- Switching between slots costs nothing measurable.

**C3: prefill chunk size.** Every chunk costs a fixed ~0.39 s, about one full read of the expert weights, so small chunks are expensive:

| chunk | worst voice wait | agent prefill cost |
|---|---|---|
| 1024 | ~1.3 s | +44% |
| 2048 | ~2.0 s | +15% |

I kept 2048 as the default (see decision 1 below).

**C1's depth check.** The same 99k-token prompt gave byte-identical answers in slot 0 and slot 1, so the attention path used at long context is correct in a non-zero slot.

**C5a: price of batching three streams.** A 3-row pass costs **1.78 steps**, not the ~1.5 hoped for. That works out to ~19 tok/s per stream instead of ~11 interleaved. Everything except the MoE stays flat as rows are added, and one MoE kernel (`moe.up`) grows 4x over three rows, so it's the one to look at in C5.
- This was measured on a scratch build with the 3-row limit raised, which also passed the correctness test.
- C5's commit should carry the two new decode-path subtests I wrote for that build. The existing 3-row test doesn't exercise the new kernels.

**C4: checkpoints, built and gated.**
- **What it does:** each slot saves its state just before the last user message. The next request with the same system prompt restores it and prefills only its own few tokens.
- **Result:** voice time to first token goes from **1.83 s to 0.19 s**. Agents finish 6 s sooner, and total throughput rises 11%.
- **Gates:**
  - Restoring gives bit-identical logits to prefilling from scratch, even after the slot ran a longer, different continuation and another slot ran in between.
  - Leaving out the DeltaNet or PLE part of the restore changes the output, so the test can fail.
  - A backend test checks that a restored request streams exactly the same text as a fresh one.
  - The neighbouring slot, rewind, speculation and scheduler tests still pass.
- **One design change from the plan:** the attention index table turned out not to need restoring. Blocks the model hasn't reached are always forced to "select" or "ignore", so stale values there can't change anything. I dropped that part and kept the test case that could have proved it wrong.
- **Also changed:** when agents need a slot, the scheduler now takes one without a checkpoint first, so they don't throw away the voice slot's saved system prompt.
- **Not built:** restoring a checkpoint into a different slot.
- **Flag:** `-llm-checkpoints` (on by default).

`CONCURRENCY.md`, `API.md` and `TODO.md` are updated. I haven't committed anything; the auto-committer will pick it up. `ai.service` is still stopped: `systemctl --user start ai` brings it back.

Two decisions for you:
1. **Chunk 2048 or 1024?** With checkpoints in, the chunk wait is now most of a voice command's delay while an agent prefills: ~2.2 s worst case against ~1.5 s. Going to 1024 makes every background prefill 25% slower and costs about 6% of total throughput.
2. **Slots for the deployed LLM.** The unit template still runs one slot. Until C6, three slots means about 112k context each instead of one 262k conversation.

node_type: memory
