---

**`go test ./llm/` needs `-timeout 60m`.** Go's default is ten minutes and the
suite runs past it inside `TestQSASelectionSurvivesOurScores`. What you get is
a panic stack and `FAIL strix-halo-vulkan/llm 600.024s`, which **reads as a
real failure and is not one**. With a warm bank cache the whole suite is
~180 s; cold it is much longer.

**`TestGraphLogits` passes as of 2026-09-22** — it now takes a near-tie on
argmax (7 tokens, "The capital of France is Paris."). Its diagnostics at
f062e28 are `result_output ... maxAbs 1.987e+00 at 19208, rms 3.314e-01`,
argmax ours 11751 vs llama.cpp 561, "0.4920 apart" — P16's three changes
reproduce them byte for byte. (The older `2.507e+00 at 141557` digits are from
before the test changed.) To get a base to diff against, a `git worktree` of
HEAD needs `models/` and `reference/out/` symlinked in (both gitignored) and
the `.spv` files copied, or the test silently prints nothing.

**That identity is also the cheapest whole-model bit-exactness check there
is.** A change that claims to be bit-exact should reproduce those numbers to
the digit through all 48 layers — stronger than any block test, and it costs
one 61 s run.

**`LLM_BANK_CACHE` is a relative path, and `go test ./llm/` resolves it
against `llm/`.** So exporting the usual
`LLM_BANK_CACHE=models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/bank-cache` and running the
tests silently builds a **23 GB** duplicate at `llm/models/`, untracked. Use
an absolute path, or `rm -rf llm/models` afterwards. The real cache
(26 GB, 199 files) is at the repo root.

**How to apply:** the useful per-change gates are
`go test ./llm/ -run 'TestAttn|TestMoEGPU|TestGraphIsAChunkSplit' -timeout 30m`
(~80 s), and run the full suite only when something broad moved. See

content.content:
## C5a — what a three-row pass costs (measured 2026-09-23)

`cmd/llm -graph -tokens 1,2,3 -layers 48 -ctx 2048` on the shipped banks
(`LLM_DENSE_BANK`/`LLM_MOE_BANK` as `cmd/serve` sets them, plus
`LLM_BANK_CACHE`). Two builds, interleaved A/B/A/B: HEAD, where
`GEMVMaxRows` is 2 and a three-row pass falls back to the GEMM, and a scratch
worktree with `MAXROWS 3` in the four GEMV shaders and `GEMVMaxRows = 3`.
The two pairs agree within 1 ms.

| rows | HEAD | MAXROWS 3 | hc | dn | attn | **moe** | head |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 29.3 ms | 29.3 ms | 3.9 | 7.2 | 2.5 | 11.0 | 2.4 |
| 2 | 38.9 (1.33x) | 41.2 (1.41x) | 4.0 | 7.6 | 2.5 | 22.3 | 2.4 |
| 3 | 106.3 (3.6x) | **52.2 (1.78x)** | 4.2 | 7.7 | 2.6 | **33.1** | 2.4 |

(block columns are the MAXROWS 3 build)

- **Three rows cost 1.78 steps, not the ~1.5 the plan hoped for.** Batched,
  three streams would get **~19 tok/s each (57 aggregate)** against ~11.5
  each interleaved, which is 1.68x the throughput. Two rows are 1.33x, so
  ~26 tok/s each and 51 aggregate.
- **Everything but the MoE is flat in rows**, as P5b found at two: hc, dn,
  attn, ple and head are all within 0.4 ms from one row to three. **The MoE
  is the whole cost**, and `moe.up` alone goes 6.0 → 14.8 → 24.0 ms. More
  rows touch more distinct experts, so some of that growth is bytes that must
  be read. But `moe.up` grows 4.0x over three rows, while `moe.down` over the
  same expert set grows 2.3x (2.6 → 6.0 ms). `moe.up` at R rows is the kernel
  to look at before C5 is priced as final.
- **Raising MAXROWS costs two rows 2.3 ms** (38.9 → 41.2, mostly `moe.up`'s
  extra accumulator). Nothing ships two-row passes today (the speculative
  loop is parked), and one row is unchanged, so C5 can raise it. It has to
  land with its rungs.
- **Correctness in the scratch build:** `TestGraphIsAChunkSplit` passes, and
  new *unpinned* "2 / 3 at a time, on the decode schedule" subtests read
  result_norm at 5.2e-4 and 6.2e-4 rms (one row: 4.5e-4; the gate's bound is
  1e-3). The existing "3 at a time" rung runs on the pinned schedule, so it
  would not see a broken three-row GEMV. **C5's commit should carry these two
  subtests.**
- **Rule 4 (background rows riding in a voice decode):** one rider costs the
  voice stream 1.33x (35 → ~26 tok/s) and two cost it 1.78x (→ ~20 tok/s). A
  spoken reply is consumed at speech rate, which is well under either, so
  riding is plausible for TTS-bound replies. It stays a knob, and it defaults
  to off, until C5 exists.

## C4 — checkpoints (done 2026-09-23)

**2026-09-23, CONCURRENCY.md C5.** C5a priced a three-row pass with
`cmd/llm -graph -tokens 1,2,3`: **52 ms, 1.78 steps**. Those three rows are
three *consecutive tokens of one sequence*, which share experts. The server's
three concurrent agents ran **64 ms a pass**. `cmd/llm -batch` (one slot a
row, each prefilled with different wikitext) reproduced the 64 ms only once
it decoded greedily. Feeding each row a fixed token also read ~54 ms, because
a row that repeats its token reads the same experts every step. Three real
conversations touch **26.8 distinct experts a layer** against 10 for one row,
and the MoE is the part of a pass that grows with rows.

**Why:** a batched pass costs the *union* of its rows' experts, and anything
that correlates the rows' tokens shrinks the union.

-batch-depth 7000` (greedy, different text per slot), and check
`PassExperts` on the printed "distinct experts" line (~10/19/27 at 1/2/3
rows). The same trap applies to any rows-vs-cost claim about the MoE,
including P5's speculative verification rows, which *are* one sequence and
so priced correctly there. See [[concurrency-loadgen-run]] and
[[two-row-regime-needs-a-graph-gate]].

content.text:
Batched decode (C5) is done. With three agents running at once, each gets **~18 tok/s instead of ~11**, and all three finish in **62 s instead of 88 s**. The preempt chunk stays at 2048, as you asked.

**48-layer results** (same hour, batching on against off):

| | agents' decode, each | agents done | total throughput |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 agents, off | 11.0-11.5 tok/s | 88.0 s | 26.2 tok/s |
| **3 agents, on** | **17.6-18.8** | **62.0 s** | **37.1** |
| 2 agents + voice, off | 16.9 / 16.4 | 61.1 s | 26.2 |
| **2 agents + voice, on** | **23.2 / 22.3** | **48.6 s** | **32.9** |

Voice commands are unchanged: 0.2 s to first token while agents decode, as after C4.

**How it works:**
- **One pass for several conversations.** The weight-heavy parts (projections, MoE, head) run over all rows together. The parts that hold a conversation's history (attention cache, DeltaNet state, PLE ring) run once per row on that conversation's slot.
- **No new kernels were needed for the per-row position.** The shaders now read it from a per-row word that ordinary passes leave at zero, so single-conversation decode is byte-for-byte what it was.
- **The scheduler batches decode steps of the same priority class**, waiting up to 5 ms for conversations still sampling. The measured gap between batched steps is 0.3 ms. Background rows still never join a voice command's pass.

**A correction to this morning's pricing.** The earlier estimate (1.78 steps for three rows) was measured on one conversation's consecutive tokens, which share experts. Three real conversations touch 26.8 experts per layer, and the first build's 3-row pass took **64 ms**, not 52.
- The cause was `moe.up`, which computed every expert tile at full row count although most tiles serve one row. It now skips the padding rows.
- That brought the 3-row pass to **53.4 ms (1.83 steps)**. The shared expert reads ~0.25 ms slower at three rows, which I haven't explained.

**Verification:**
- Every batched row's logits are **bit-identical** to that conversation stepped alone, at 3 rows and at 2. Corrupting any one block's per-row position changes the output, so the test can fail.
- The full `llm` suite passes, and the whole-model logits check reproduces this morning's numbers to the digit.
- Raising the 3-row limit broke three older tests, all on stale assumptions, and I fixed them. Two MoE tests had a "refused past the limit" check that was passing for the wrong reason.

**Other additions:**
- `cmd/llm -batch` benchmarks batched passes the realistic way (a different conversation per slot, decoding greedily).
- `-llm-batch-decode` is the on/off switch, used as the control above.

Solo decode reads 33.8 tok/s this afternoon against 34.7 this morning. A same-hour comparison against this morning's binaries puts the one-row pass at 29.0 → 29.5 ms, inside run-to-run noise, so it's drift, not these changes.

`CONCURRENCY.md` (new C5 section plus the C5a correction), `TODO.md` and `API.md` are updated. Nothing is committed yet: the auto-committer hasn't run since this morning, so the C4 and C5 work is all in the working tree. `ai.service` is still stopped.

One decision is yours: **slots × context for the deployed server.** Three slots means ~112k tokens per conversation, instead of one at 262k. If the agents need more, that's C6 (full context in every slot), which is the next stage in the plan.

content.text:
C6 is done: the server now holds **three conversations, each with the full 262,144-token context**. The unit template's LLM line is set to `-llm-slots 3`.

**How it works:** each slot now has its own K, V and indexer buffers, and its own set of attention pipelines bound to them. Switching slots swaps both.
- That makes the 4 GiB buffer limit apply per slot, so three full-context slots fit where the shared buffers allowed about 349k tokens in total.
- No shader changed, so this went faster than the plan's approach, which needed the slot index inside every kernel.
- Building the pipelines three times costs nothing measurable: the server comes up in 68 s, against 66 s with one slot.
- Batched decode needed no changes.

**Verification:**
- **New slot test:** slot 2 prefills half a prompt, slot 0 runs something else, and slot 2 continues. The result is bit-identical to running slot 2 with nothing in between. In a control that makes slot 2 read slot 0's cache, the output changes from the first continued token.
  - My first version of this control passed when it should have failed: a fresh prompt overwrites every cell it reads, so sharing is invisible without a continuation.
- **Existing cache-size test:** extended to run in slot 2 of three after slot 0 has been used. Still bit-identical.
- **Full model, the served config:** a 237,231-token prompt in slot 2 recalls "Robert Boulter", and the same prompt in slot 0 gives a byte-identical answer. Decode at that depth is 30.1 tok/s.
- **Load mix:** agents decode at 21.4-22.9 tok/s each, and voice commands are unchanged.
- The full `llm` suite, the backend tests and `go vet` all pass. The whole-model logits check still matches this morning to the digit.

**Two costs you'll see, neither caused by C6:**
- **Memory:** about 98 GB resident, leaving 19 GB free on this box.
- **Long-prompt prefill is ~12% slower** (901 tok/s against 1022 for the 237k prompt). With more than one slot, background prefills run in 2048-token chunks, the trade you chose. A request marked interactive isn't chunked, if one long prompt ever needs the full rate.
- **A 262k-token cache doubles attention cost during prefill, even on an empty cache**: 366 ms per 2048-token chunk against 178 ms at 65k. This morning's binary measures the same to 3 ms, so it has been there since the 262k context went in. One prefill kernel still scales with the cache's size rather than the tokens in it, which costs about 10% of every prefill at the served context. I've listed it as the next lever in `CONCURRENCY.md`.

Everything is written up in `CONCURRENCY.md` (C6 section, decisions, next steps), `API.md`, `TODO.md` and the unit template. Nothing is committed yet. `ai.service` is still stopped. On this box its active line serves the other verticals, so the new LLM line takes effect wherever you deploy the LLM machine.
